newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile ratifies trade deal with Canada.
newsitem.headline: Chile ratifies trade deal with Canada.

text.p: The Chilean Senate gave final approval on Wednesday to a free trade agreement with Canada, putting the treaty into effect and laying the groundwork for Chile's long-delayed entrance into NAFTA.
The agreement sweeps away tariffs on about 80 percent of trade between the two countries immediately and will phase out the rest over the next 18 years.
Chilean officials have said the treaty could boost bilateral trade, currently about $670 million a year, by about five times over the next decade.
The agreement is the most far-reaching and complex of a series of free trade deals Chile, with Latin America's strongest economy, has reached with various countries and blocs in the last three years.
"This is a historic moment for Chile. We have negotiated as equals with a Group of Seven country," said Finance Minister Eduardo Aninat after the vote.
The agreement also makes it easier for either country's companies to invest in the other. Canada is already Chile's second-largest investor, with about $8 billion invested, mainly in mining.

But the treaty's main impact may be to set the basic terms for Chile's later inclusion in the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) as its fourth partner after the United States, Mexico and Canada.
The treaty, with language similar to NAFTA's, has been called "NAFTA Light."
"This agreement based on the NAFTA model is an investment in growth for people on both the trade and investment side," Canadian Ambassador Marc Lortie said.

"Canada doesn't have many free trade agreements and it's the first time we've signed one with a country in South America, so it's really giving direction to our private sector. This gives them a tremendous incentive to come to South America."

Chile's long-standing invitation to join NAFTA has been stalled in the U.S. Congress, where lawmakers have so far failed to approve fast-track powers for U.S. negotiators. Fast-track would allow trade officials to negotiate a trade treaty without fear of it being later amended in Congress.
But if fast-track is approved and negotiations for Chile's entrance into NAFTA begin, officials on both sides say the Canadian agreement should make talks smoother.
"In every sense this is a positive agreement. It leaves us on a good footing to reach a trade agreement later with the United States," said Christian Democrat senator Andres Zaldivar.
Opposition to the agreement came mainly from rightist senators representing farm districts in southern Chile, where their constituents fear they will be hurt by Canadian agricultural imports.

"Maybe this agreement has some positive effects, but it's highly negative for our agriculture, for the south and the people who live there," said rightist senator Bruno Siebert, one of six senators voting against the agreement. Thirty-four voted in favor.
In a bow to farm groups, tariffs on a range of agricultural products ranging from cheese to eggs to meat will be the last to come down, some staying into effect well into the next century.
Chilean grain farmers are still fuming over the free trade pact with the Mercosur bloc signed last year, which they claim will flood them with cheap Argentine and Brazilian cereals.
